newsitem.title: USA: Market shrugs off drop in US March housing starts.
newsitem.headline: Market shrugs off drop in US March housing starts.

text.p: The pace of U.S. housing starts pulled back in March from February's weather-induced torrid clip, but immediate market reaction was muted as the data did little to change the overall economic outlook, analysts said on Wednesday.
"It's a litte bit softer than we and others were looking for, but certainly the direction is as expected," said Mike Niemira, an economist at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi.
"By and large, the two months together are still favorable and the picture really hasn't changed," he added.

The Commerce Department said construction starts on new homes and apartments fell 6.4 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.425 million units in March after a revised 10.7 percent surge in February to 1.522 million units a year.
A 20.2 percent drop in Midwest housing starts was the largest decline since January 1994 and nationwide, the drop was slightly larger than expected.
A Reuter poll of economists had forecast a 4.45 percent decline in March to 1.46 million units after atypical spring-like weather prompted a surge in February starts.
"The data suggest the housing sector is growing, but not as fast as the rest of the economy," said Matt Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.
"The housing sector is not an engine for economic growth. It will be a follower, not a leader," he added.
However, BancAmerica Securities Inc economists said average housing starts for 1997, including March, only slightly trailed the pace set in all of 1996, a "robust year."
"Housing should continue to boost gross domestic product in the second quarter," said Steven Wood, managing director.
Economists were hesitant to attribute the above-forecast March decline to a recent back-up in U.S. interest rates.
"It's too soon, too soon, too soon. It takes a while for people to get acclimated to higher rates and all that," said Robert Brusca, chief economists at Nikko Securities Co International Inc.
If rates continue to rise, the effects on starts could be seen in the second quarter at the earliest, economists said.
Federal Reserve policymakers raised the federal funds rate target 25 basis points to 5.5 percent on March 25.
The March slowdown in starts will have little impact on future Fed monetary policy decisions, experts said.
"The Fed is much more concerned with consumer spending on non-durables and services than they are on run-away housing price inflation or something along those lines," Alexy said.

Reaction in the U.S. Treasury and foreign exchange markets to the data had been muted. The benchmark 30-year Treasury had inched lower, with dealers hesitant to significantly change their positions ahead of the 0915 EDT/1315 GMT release of March U.S. industrial production and capacity utilization.
"It was almost a yawner, probably because it doesn't change the storyline so the markets are not paying much attention to it," Niemira said.
